q: A point moves through an arc of length s on a circle of radius r. Its angular displacement θ in radians is given by:
x: Angle in radians is arc length divided by radius, θ = s/r. Multiplying s by r or including 2π are common slips.

q: A point on a fan blade 0.25 m from the axis travels along an arc of 1.5 m. Through what angle has the blade turned?
x: θ = s/r = 1.5/0.25 = 6 rad. Multiplying the two numbers gives 0.375, which is wrong.

q: Through what angle does the second hand of a clock turn in 15 seconds?
x: The second hand makes one revolution (2π rad) in 60 s, so in 15 s it turns 15/60 × 2π = π/2 rad.

q: A flywheel turns through an angular displacement of 4π rad. How many complete turns has it made?
x: Each turn is 2π rad, so 4π rad corresponds to 4π/2π = 2 turns.

q: Large angular displacements are not treated as vectors because they do not obey the:
o: Rule that a vector has a magnitude
Rule for multiplying a vector by a number
x: The result of two large rotations depends on the order in which they are done, so they do not add commutatively. Only very small angular displacements behave as vectors.

q: A cyclist rides 314 m along a circular track of radius 50 m. Taking π = 3.14, his angular displacement about the centre is:
o: 0.16 rad, a small fraction of a revolution
x: θ = s/r = 314/50 = 6.28 rad = 2π rad, which is exactly one revolution. Dividing the radius by the arc gives the wrong 0.16.

q: Taking one rotation of the Earth as 24 hours, through what angle does the Earth turn about its axis in 4 hours?
x: In 4 hours the Earth makes 4/24 = 1/6 of a turn, so it turns 2π/6 = π/3 rad.

q: A complete revolution, expressed in degrees, is:
x: One complete revolution is 360°, which is the same as 2π rad. 57.3° is the size of one radian.

q: How many radians are there in 45°?
x: Multiply degrees by π/180: 45 × π/180 = π/4 rad.

q: An angle of π/3 rad expressed in degrees is:
A door swings open through a quarter turn. In radians this angle is:
x: A full revolution is 2π rad, so one quarter of it is 2π/4 = π/2 rad (90°).

q: A wheel makes 2.5 revolutions. The angle it turns through, in degrees, is:
x: Each revolution is 360°, so 2.5 × 360° = 900°.

q: Taking 1 rad ≈ 57.3°, an angle of 0.5 rad is approximately:
x: 0.5 × 57.3° ≈ 28.6°. Doubling instead of halving gives 114.6°.

q: Which statement about units of angle is correct?
o: One revolution is equal to π rad
One degree is 1/360 of a revolution
The degree is the SI unit of angle
x: The degree is defined as 1/360 of a full revolution. π rad (not 1 rad) equals 180°, a revolution is 2π rad, and the SI unit of angle is the radian.

q: Angular velocity of a rotating body is defined as the:
o: Rate of change of linear velocity
Rate of change of angular displacement
Product of radius and angular displacement
x: Angular velocity ω = Δθ/Δt, the rate at which angular displacement changes. Rate of change of linear velocity is linear acceleration.

q: A ceiling fan rotates at 300 revolutions per minute. Its angular velocity is:
x: 300 rev min⁻¹ = 5 rev s⁻¹; ω = 2π × 5 = 10π rad s⁻¹. Forgetting the 2π gives 5 rad s⁻¹.

q: A body moves uniformly in a circle with time period T. Its angular speed is:
x: In one period the body turns through 2π rad, so ω = 2π/T.

q: The angular speed of the second hand of a clock is:
x: The second hand turns 2π rad in 60 s, so ω = 2π/60 = π/30 rad s⁻¹.

q: A wheel rotates clockwise as seen by an observer facing it. By the right-hand rule, its angular velocity points:
o: Along the axle, towards the observer
Along the tangent to the rim
Along the axle, away from the observer
x: Curl the right-hand fingers clockwise (as seen); the thumb points away from the observer along the axle. Angular velocity is always along the axis.

q: A satellite completes one orbit every 90 minutes. Taking π = 3.14, its angular velocity is about:
x: T = 90 × 60 = 5400 s, ω = 2π/T = 6.28/5400 ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻³ rad s⁻¹. Using minutes instead of seconds gives 7.0 × 10⁻².

q: An angular velocity of 1 rad s⁻¹ is closest to:
x: 1 rad s⁻¹ = 60 rad min⁻¹ = 60/2π ≈ 9.5 rev min⁻¹.

q: For a point at distance r from the axis of a body with angular acceleration α, the tangential acceleration is:
x: Linear and angular quantities are linked by the radius: s = rθ, v = rω and a = rα.

q: The angular velocity of a wheel rises uniformly from 10 rad s⁻¹ to 30 rad s⁻¹ in 4 s. Its angular acceleration is:
x: Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity: α = Δω/Δt = (30 − 10)/4 = 5 rad s⁻².

q: A point on the rim of a pulley of radius 0.2 m moves at 6 m s⁻¹. The angular speed of the pulley is:
x: ω = v/r = 6/0.2 = 30 rad s⁻¹. Multiplying v by r gives 1.2, which is wrong.

q: A disc of radius 0.3 m turns through 5 rad. How far does a point on its edge travel along its circular path?
x: s = rθ = 0.3 × 5 = 1.5 m. Dividing 5 by 0.3 gives 16.7, which is wrong.

q: Starting from rest, a grinding disc of radius 0.25 m speeds up at 4 rad s⁻². Three seconds later, what are its tangential acceleration and its rim speed?
x: a = rα = 0.25 × 4 = 1 m s⁻². After 3 s, ω = αt = 12 rad s⁻¹, so v = rω = 0.25 × 12 = 3 m s⁻¹.

q: A stone on a string is whirled in a circle at a fixed angular speed. If the string is made twice as long, the linear speed of the stone:
x: v = rω; with ω fixed, doubling r doubles v.

q: For a particle in uniform circular motion, which statement about directions is correct?
o: Both linear and angular velocity are along the tangent
Linear velocity is along the radius; angular velocity is along the tangent
Both linear and angular velocity point towards the centre
Linear velocity is along the tangent; angular velocity is along the axis
x: The linear velocity is tangent to the circle, while angular velocity is a vector along the axis of rotation, given by the right-hand rule.
